blocks.c: In the silence after the photocopier stopped, a voice said:

It was the clerk's handwriting made audible, if that means anything: small, neat, old-fashioned, unhurried, coming from about ten feet behind me at the height of a person's head, and there was nothing behind me, because I turned round with the torch and there was a rack of boxes and dust and nothing else.

"They were yours. They were surrendered." A pause. "Not by contract. By inattention. Which is a legitimate mode of surrender in every jurisdiction we have ever operated in, and we have operated in eleven."

Here is a thing I have learned about being frightened. There is a layer under the panic where you are still, technically, a person with a job, and if you can get down to that layer you can operate. It is not courage. It is closer to filling in a form while a fire alarm goes off.
I got down to that layer.
I got my book out. I got my pen out. My hands were doing something I had no control over, but you can write with shaking hands; it just looks bad.

"03:52," I said out loud, writing it. "Minus nine. Entity claims three items surrendered by inattention. I dispute it. All three are logged in the front of this book under OUTSTANDING, dated the sixteenth, five days before this conversation."
The silence went on for a long, long time.
Then the voice said, in a completely different tone — and I swear to you it was the tone of a man at a counter discovering that the customer has, unusually, brought the receipt:
"...Show me the front of the book."
